lesson.title: Knocking and Shaking Hands: The Connect Operation
lesson.summary: The connect operation is the client side call that reaches out to a server's socket address and, for TCP, actually carries out the three way handshake that establishes the connection.
lesson.body:
connect() is the client-side operation that initiates a connection to a server at a given socket address. For a TCP socket, this call is what actually carries out the three-way handshake, the mechanism that establishes the connection in the first place.

It is worth noticing how much simpler the client side is compared to the server side. The server needs bind(), listen(), and accept(), in that order, just to be ready to receive anything at all. The client, by contrast, needs only socket() followed directly by connect(), because the client already knows the socket address it wants to reach, typically supplied by the application itself, a URL's host name resolved to an address and a default port, for example, rather than being something the client has to claim in advance the way a server claims a port.

One detail worth calling out: a client does not normally call bind() itself before calling connect(). The operating system automatically assigns the socket a local IP address, based on routing, and an unused ephemeral port at the moment connect() is called, unless the application specifically bound the socket to something beforehand. This is exactly why clients do not need well known ports the way servers do, tying back to why bind() mattered mainly on the server side.

connect() blocks until the handshake either completes or fails outright. It can return an error such as connection refused, meaning no process was listening at that address at all, in other words nobody had called listen() there, or it can time out if no response ever comes back, perhaps because a firewall is blocking the attempt or the host is simply unreachable.

Bringing the whole lifecycle together as a capstone: a server runs socket(), bind() to 192.0.2.50:9000, listen(), and then sits waiting inside accept(). A client runs socket() and then connect() to that same address, 192.0.2.50:9000. The client's connect() call and the server's pending accept() call are two sides of the exact same handshake. Once it completes, the client's original socket becomes the client's end of the connection, and the server's accept() call returns a brand new socket that is the server's end of that same connection, entirely distinct from the listening socket, which is still sitting there waiting for the next one to arrive. From this point on, both sides simply call send() and recv() on their respective sockets to exchange data, and the whole setup phase spanning this chapter and the three before it is complete.
